analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all earnings and raises seniors' cost-of-living adjustments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 31, 2025 with two Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it; the current 2025 cap on taxed earnings is $176,100.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would phase out the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes. Today, earnings above $176,100 (in 2025) are not taxed for Social Security; under the bill, the portion above the cap would be taxed at a shrinking share each year — 86% of it in 2026, falling to zero exempted by 2032, when all earnings would be taxed [S2] [S3]. It would also count those high earnings slightly in the benefit formula, and it would switch Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment to an index reflecting the spending of people 62 and older, which typically rises faster than the current index [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries gain through larger annual cost-of-living increases tied to elderly spending patterns [S2]. Low-income beneficiaries are protected twice over: any benefit increase from the new index cannot be counted as income that reduces their Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income benefits [S2] [S3]. All current and future beneficiaries gain from the program's improved finances, since taxing all earnings brings in substantial new revenue. Current workers earning under the cap pay no more than they do today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Phases out the taxable maximum so that all earnings are subject to Social Security payroll taxes after 2031, raising revenue and strengthening the program's finances [S2] [S3].

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the spending habits of people 62 and older, and directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish that index [S2] [S3].

Prevents any benefit increase from the new index from counting as income for Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income eligibility, so low-income beneficiaries do not lose other assistance because their Social Security check went up [S2] [S3].

Includes high earners' above-cap earnings in the benefit formula at modest rates (a 3% factor and a 0.25% factor on surplus earnings), so high earners receive some additional benefit for the extra taxes they pay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households and self-employed people with earnings above roughly $176,100 per year pay more, with the share of above-cap earnings taxed rising from 86% in 2026 to 100% after 2031 [S2] [S3]. Self-employed high earners pay both the employee and employer shares. High earners receive only a small increase in their own future benefits in return, so most of the new revenue functions as funding for the program overall rather than as a return on their own contributions [S3].

drawbacks.text: It is a large tax increase on high earners: a household earning $500,000 would eventually pay Social Security payroll tax on the full amount above the cap, and self-employed high earners pay both the employee and employer shares on top of it [S2] [S3].

High earners get very little back for the extra taxes: only 3% and 0.25% factors apply to their above-cap earnings in the benefit formula, so the bill is largely a redistribution of revenue rather than a matching contribution-to-benefit arrangement [S3].
The elderly cost-of-living index has historically risen somewhat faster than the index now used, which would add to the program's long-term benefit costs, partly offsetting the new revenue [S2].

A good-faith objection is that applying payroll taxes to all earnings without a proportional benefit changes Social Security's character from insurance-for-contributions toward a transfer program, which critics argue could affect support for the program among higher-income taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a large tax increase on roughly the top slice of earners for larger annual benefit increases for every Social Security beneficiary and stronger program financing. For the roughly nine in ten workers who earn under the cap, the cost is zero and the benefit is a faster-growing check. For high earners the cost is substantial and the individual return small. The main design weakness is that the richer cost-of-living index raises costs at the same time as the new revenue comes in, so the net improvement in solvency depends on the balance between the two.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate on July 31, 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on July 31, 2025, joined by Senators Tina Smith and Jeff Merkley as cosponsors [S3] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Social Security taxes and benefits [S1] [S5].
The committee's action history for the bill ends with the referral; no hearing, markup, or vote has been recorded [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has benefited or been harmed by an outcome yet, since the bill has not advanced or died. If it follows the usual path of similar bills, the people better off under the current stalemate are high earners who would pay substantially more in payroll taxes under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — nothing has happened

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 31, 2025.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 31, 2025; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote since [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats are on record in support and there has been no vote, so the partisan shape of the fight has not yet been tested; Social Security tax-cap legislation has historically split along party lines.

industries.note: They would pay Social Security payroll tax on earnings above the roughly $176,100 cap, phasing in to all earnings by 2032, and would receive only a small increase in their own benefits in return [S2] [S3]. Their financial interest in blocking the bill runs against beneficiaries' interest in larger checks and stronger program financing.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries (retirees and disability recipients)
industries.note: All beneficiaries would receive cost-of-living adjustments tied to elderly spending patterns, which typically rise faster than the current index, and the program's finances would be strengthened by the new revenue [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With three Senate sponsors, no House companion momentum indicated in the record, and no hearing or markup in the Finance Committee more than a year before the Congress ends, the bill is unlikely to advance without a major shift; bills raising the Social Security tax cap routinely stall in the Finance Committee. Its realistic path is to remain in committee and expire at the end of the 119th Congress unless its sponsors build substantially broader support.
